analysis.one_liner: Fast-tracks federal permitting for mines producing strategic minerals by narrowing environmental reviews and lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 254-177 on October 22, 2015, with all 246 voting Republicans in favor and only 8 of 188 Democrats; the Senate never voted on it and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs federal agencies to speed up permits for mines that produce minerals deemed strategic and critical. It lets an agency declare that environmental review requirements under the National Environmental Policy Act are already satisfied, sets a 30-month ceiling on the review process for some projects, exempts parts of National Forests from special-area rules, and makes it much harder to challenge mine permits in court: lawsuits must be filed within 60 days, courts cannot order broad fixes, and plaintiffs cannot recover their legal fees from the government. Supporters said 7-to-10-year permitting delays were driving the U.S. to depend on foreign minerals; opponents said it strips communities of their main tools to hold mining projects accountable.
analysis.who_benefits: Mining companies holding or seeking permits on federal land gain faster approvals, predictable timelines negotiated with agencies, easier access to mineral areas in National Forests, and far less risk that lawsuits by opponents will delay or reshape projects.

how_it_helps.text: Declares that mine permits for strategic and critical minerals are 'infrastructure projects' eligible for streamlined federal permitting coordination.

Deems National Environmental Policy Act requirements satisfied if the lead agency determines any state or federal agency has addressed or will address the required environmental factors, with a written decision due within 90 days of the application.
Requires agencies to sign scheduling agreements with project proponents and caps the total review process at 30 months unless the parties agree to extend it.
Exempts identified mineral resources in National Forests from federal Special Areas regulations and keeps those exemptions in place after a mine's plan of operations is approved.

Bars lawsuits over mine permits unless filed within 60 days, limits the remedies courts can order, allows permit holders to intervene in any challenge, and eliminates federal payment of attorneys' fees under the Equal Access to Justice Act for these cases.
Declares that the lead agency's priority in evaluating permits is to maximize mineral development while mitigating environmental impacts.

analysis.who_pays: Communities near proposed mines lose their strongest check on project approvals, since environmental review can be declared satisfied by the permitting agency itself and court challenges are narrowed, time-limited, and unaffordable for most plaintiffs without fee recovery. The public also bears the environmental consequences of faster mine development on federal land.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets the permitting agency itself declare environmental review requirements satisfied, which removes an independent check before mines are approved on federal land.

A 60-day filing deadline plus the loss of fee recovery under the Equal Access to Justice Act would make it practically impossible for most citizens, tribes, or conservation groups to challenge a flawed mine permit in court.
The bill states the permitting agency's priority is to 'maximize the development of the mineral resource,' tilting the legal standard for every permit decision toward extraction.

Fair objection to acknowledge: the findings in the bill document real problems, including U.S. import dependence rising from 45 to 65 nonfuel mineral commodities since 1990 and 7-to-10-year permitting delays ranked the biggest risk to U.S. mining projects, so some permitting reform is a legitimate goal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill targets is real: mineral import dependence grew and permitting can take years, and a genuine coordination-and-timelines bill could help both manufacturers and mining towns. But this version goes well beyond coordination: it lets the permitting agency certify its own environmental review as complete, caps reviews at 30 months, exempts forest mineral areas from special protections, and closes the courthouse door to most challengers by combining a 60-day deadline with a ban on fee recovery. The savings in time come largely by removing the public's ability to slow or shape a project, so the cost lands on the communities and landscapes where mines are actually built.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 254-177 in October 2015, but after the Senate referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee no vote ever happened, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced April 22, 2015, by Rep. Mark Amodei with 48 cosponsors, all Republicans.
The House Natural Resources Committee ordered the bill reported 23-14 and reported it on September 8, 2015, with the Judiciary Committee discharged the same day.
On October 22, 2015, a rule for floor consideration passed, Democratic amendments from Reps. Lowenthal, Dingell, and Cartwright failed, and a Republican amendment was adopted.
A motion by Rep. Peters to recommit the bill with instructions failed 184-246, with all 245 voting Republicans opposed and 184 of 185 voting Democrats in favor.
The House passed the bill 254-177, with all 246 voting Republicans in favor and only 8 of 188 voting Democrats in favor.

The Senate received the bill on October 26, 2015, and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, where no further action was recorded before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Communities near mining projects and conservation groups kept the existing environmental review rules and full access to the courts, since the bill never became law; mining companies, meanwhile, gained nothing and continued operating under the slower permitting process the bill was meant to replace.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities and conservation groups kept current rules

sides.party_line_note: The final vote split almost perfectly by party: all 246 voting Republicans voted yes while only 8 of 188 voting Democrats did, and the motion to recommit failed 184-246 on nearly the mirror-image split.

industries.note: The bill speeds and simplifies federal permits, opens more National Forest land to mining access, and makes court challenges by opponents slow, narrow, and costly. The faster approvals come largely by removing the environmental review and litigation tools that nearby communities rely on.

The 60-day filing deadline, limits on court-ordered relief, and ban on Equal Access to Justice Act fee recovery would make it financially impossible for most of these groups to challenge mine permits on behalf of the public.
